title: Cache Coherence Protocols
summary: The multicore coherence problem, snooping vs directory-based solutions, and the MESI protocol that most CPUs implement.

slides.subTitle: Multiple copies, one truth
slides.markdown:
Every core has its own private cache, and several cores can hold a **copy of the same line** at once. If one core writes its copy without telling anyone, other cores keep reading stale data forever — silently wrong results with no error thrown.

**Cache coherence** is the hardware protocol that prevents this: it keeps every core's view of a given memory address consistent, so a write by one core eventually becomes visible to reads by every other core.

slides.subTitle: Single-writer-or-multiple-readers
slides.markdown:
Coherence enforces one core rule: at any moment, for a given address, either **one core has a writable copy** or **any number of cores have read-only copies** — never both at once. And any write eventually becomes visible to every other core's later reads.

This is deliberately a *per-address* guarantee — it says nothing about the relative order of writes to *different* addresses across cores. That broader question is memory consistency, covered separately (and often conflated with coherence, in the pitfall below).

slides.subTitle: Every cache watches the bus
slides.markdown:
In **snooping**, every core's cache controller watches ("snoops") a shared bus for every other core's memory transactions. When a core wants to write a line, it **broadcasts** that intent; every other core's cache checks whether it has a copy and invalidates it if so.

This works well at small core counts, where a shared bus can carry the broadcast traffic — but broadcasting scales poorly, since every write from every core is announced to every other core whether or not they care.

slides.subTitle: Four states per line
slides.markdown:
**MESI** tags every cache line with one of four states: **Modified** (this core has the only copy, and it's been written — dirty), **Exclusive** (this core has the only copy, unmodified — matches memory), **Shared** (multiple cores may have read-only copies, all matching memory), **Invalid** (this line doesn't hold valid data).

Transitions between these states are triggered by local reads/writes and by snooped requests from other cores, and together they implement exactly the single-writer-or-multiple-readers guarantee from before.

slides.subTitle: A MESI walk-through
slides.markdown:
Two cores reading, then one writing, shows the full state dance.

![A MESI state-transition walk for one cache line across a read/write sequence from two cores](assets/mesi-transitions.svg)

Core 1 reads first (Exclusive, since no one else has it), Core 2 also reads (both drop to Shared), then Core 1 writes (its copy goes Modified, Core 2's is invalidated) — exactly enforcing single-writer-or-multiple-readers.

slides.subTitle: Replacing broadcast with bookkeeping
slides.markdown:
**Directory-based** coherence replaces the broadcast with a central (or distributed) **directory** that tracks, per line, exactly which cores hold a copy and in what state. A write only needs to message the cores actually listed in the directory, not every core on the system.

This is what lets coherence scale to systems with dozens or hundreds of cores, where a shared broadcast bus would be hopelessly congested — at the cost of directory storage and an extra indirection to consult it.

slides.subTitle: Snooping vs directory
slides.markdown:
| Mechanism | Traffic pattern | Scales to | Overhead |
|---|---|---|---|
| Snooping | Broadcast every transaction to every cache | Small core counts (a handful to ~dozens) | Bus bandwidth used by every core's traffic, whether interested or not |
| Directory-based | Targeted messages only to cores holding a copy | Large core counts (dozens to hundreds+) | Directory storage, plus an indirection to consult it |

**How to decide:** snooping's simplicity wins while a shared bus can still carry full broadcast traffic. Past that point, the directory's extra storage and lookup cost is worth paying to avoid congesting every core with irrelevant broadcasts — which is why large multicore/multi-socket systems use directories almost universally.

slides.subTitle: Coherence is not consistency
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "If my caches are coherent, my multithreaded program's memory operations will appear in a sane, predictable order."

**Why it's wrong:** coherence only guarantees agreement about a **single address**. It says nothing about the relative *ordering* of writes to **different** addresses across cores — that's **memory consistency**, a separate guarantee.

**Correct model:** a fully coherent system can still reorder operations on different addresses in surprising ways — that's why memory barriers/fences exist (cross-link: memory-consistency-models).
